project: RetailOps: An MCP-Based Enterprise Decision Orchestration Framework for Autonomous Retail Operations

records.claim: Flowr decomposes supermarket supply chain operations into specialized AI agents coordinated by a central reasoning LLM and incorporates an MCP-enabled supervisory interface.
records.source: Bandara et al. (2026), 'Flowr -- Scaling Up Retail Supply Chain Operations Through Agentic AI in Large Scale Supermarket Chains', arXiv:2604.05987
records.comparison_relevance: Demonstrates independent adoption of MCP in enterprise retail supply chain orchestration.

records.claim: The reviewed public source provides the academic description of Flowr, but the present comparison did not establish access to a complete reproducible implementation, equivalent datasets, and the full experimental environment.
records.comparison_relevance: Defines the boundary of comparative reproducibility.

records.claim: WorkflowLLM constructs WorkflowBench (106,763 samples, 1,503 APIs) and trains WorkflowLlama to evaluate dynamic workflow generation and tool orchestration.
records.source: Fan et al. (ICLR 2025), 'WorkflowLLM: Enhancing Workflow Orchestration Capability of Large Language Models', arXiv:2411.02052
records.comparison_relevance: Exemplifies dynamic generative planning versus explicit DAG state-machine orchestration.

records.claim: Proposes an autonomous multi-agent AI system combining LLMs and reinforcement learning for retail inventory replenishment, evaluated in a middle-scale mart setting.
records.source: Syed et al. (2025), 'Agentic AI Framework for Smart Inventory Replenishment', arXiv:2511.23366
records.comparison_relevance: Illustrates domain decision-quality evaluation (stockouts, holding costs) distinct from software systems orchestration metrics.

records.claim: Coordinates a sequential 5-stage retail decision pipeline via an explicit LangGraph StateGraph DAG connecting microservices over FastMCP STDIO transport.
records.comparison_relevance: Defines core RetailOps architectural topology and protocol interface.

records.claim: Demonstrated service replacement with 0 lines of code modified in existing sibling services and 100% downstream decision consumption.

Persistent MCP session pooling reduced repeated process initialization costs, yielding a mean workflow latency of 37.75 ms compared to 11,489.28 ms for process-per-call execution in the evaluated test environment.
records.comparison_relevance: Quantifies process lifecycle amortization and runtime performance.

records.claim: Evaluated across 6 failure scenarios with 100% failure detection, 100% downstream protection aborts via failed_enrichment, and 0 zombie processes verified via psutil.
records.comparison_relevance: Quantifies fault tolerance and OS subprocess resource cleanup.

records.claim: Integrated a 5th specialized service (Supplier Intelligence) with 0 modifications to existing service code, 183 LOC in the new service, and complete field-by-field output parity across 11 fields.
records.comparison_relevance: Quantifies developer effort and architectural extensibility.

records.claim: RetailOps and Flowr occupy complementary tiers of the retail enterprise stack: RetailOps provides high-performance, fault-isolated systems execution, while Flowr provides high-level cognitive supervisory governance.
records.comparison_relevance: Conceptual synthesis of enterprise AI orchestration paradigms.
